ratings.rationale: Unauthenticated fabricated emissions can create false targets. STRONG checks may detect inconsistent solutions, whereas WEAK conditions permit undetected deception. ADS-B attacks are experimentally established, but satellite-specific evidence is less certain; one fabricated aircraft is the conservative affected-user estimate.
ratings.issue: Cross-check effectiveness depends on whether fabricated messages can be associated with sufficiently consistent independent measurements.

ratings.rationale: Replay reintroduces genuine but stale emissions, potentially producing displaced tracks or deceptive targets. It is distinct from fabrication because the underlying message is genuine. Experimental terrestrial ADS-B evidence supports feasibility, not equivalent LEO detection performance.
ratings.issue: The record conflates replay with displacement: replay location, freshness and association determine whether a wrong track actually results.

ratings.rationale: The aircraft broadcasts a false self-reported position while independent arrival measurements remain consistent with its real location. This is principally tampering with reported content, not temporal integrity. The cross-check is the relevant defence; weak-pass conditions permit an undetected discrepancy.
ratings.issue: The stated masking chain is underspecified. A false broadcast position alone does not defeat independent localisation or establish a nominal integrity verdict.

ratings.rationale: In-band interference degrades reception and can remove surveillance coverage. RF interference against ADS-B is experimentally supported, although LEO-specific effects remain analogue evidence. The RF front end and processor are affected; interference is detectable at L1 through degraded reception and noise conditions.
ratings.issue: The footprint-wide affected-user estimate is conditional on interference extent; the record does not distinguish localised from constellation-wide denial.

missing_threats.title: RF front-end deception and AOA manipulation
missing_threats.why: Angle-of-arrival measurement integrity can fail independently of message authenticity or decoding availability.

missing_threats.title: Payload extraction and measurement tampering
missing_threats.why: Compromised extraction firmware or measurement processing can corrupt TOA, FOA and AOA before reports enter L2.

missing_threats.title: Onboard oscillator drift or manipulation
missing_threats.why: Clock drift and timing manipulation can systematically bias multiple observables independently of aircraft behaviour.

missing_threats.title: GNSS timing and positioning compromise
missing_threats.why: GNSS compromise can corrupt both onboard timing and reported aircraft positions, creating distinct downstream consequences.

rubric_ambiguities: Replay may constitute spoofing, tampering or both; the distinction depends on whether the threat concerns source attribution or modification of an existing observation.
The evidence rubric does not clearly distinguish experimentally demonstrated terrestrial ADS-B attacks from evidence demonstrated on satellite hardware.
Di_strong and Di_weak lack a precise rule for detection when the integrity monitor detects an anomaly but does not reliably identify its cause.
Affected-user scoring does not specify whether several aircraft sharing one footprint constitute regional denial or several-aircraft impact.
The damage rubric assigns displacement and deception different values, although a fabricated target may simultaneously cause both.
batch_comments.overall: All four records describe distinct, plausible threats. Fabrication, replay and false self-reported position should remain separate because their measurement consistency and detection properties differ. Jamming is a conventional availability threat. The principal weakness is extrapolating terrestrial ADS-B evidence to LEO multilateration without clearly separating demonstrated mechanisms from architecture-specific consequences.
